transcription.tex: \textbf{The modulus of a number}\par The modulus of \(a\), written \(\lvert a\rvert\), is its non-negative numerical value.\[\lvert6\rvert=6,\qquad\lvert-7.1\rvert=7.1.\]\[\lvert a\rvert=\begin{cases}a,&a\ge0,\\-a,&a<0.\end{cases}\]

\textbf{Distance and magnitude}\par The distance between two numbers \(a\) and \(b\) is \(\lvert b-a\rvert\), regardless of their order.\par For example, the distance between 2 and 7 is\[\lvert7-2\rvert=\lvert2-7\rvert=5.\]\par Modulus measures size: distances and speeds are non-negative. The same notation \(\lvert\mathbf a\rvert\) gives the magnitude (length) of a vector.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: If \(f(x)=\lvert2x-3\rvert+1\), find:
\textbf{(a)} \(f(5)\)
\[\begin{aligned}f(5)&=\lvert10-3\rvert+1\\&=7+1=8.\end{aligned}\]
\[\begin{aligned}f(-2)&=\lvert-4-3\rvert+1\\&=7+1=8.\end{aligned}\]
\textbf{(c)} \(f(1)\)
\[\begin{aligned}f(1)&=\lvert2-3\rvert+1\\&=1+1=2.\end{aligned}\]

\textbf{How to sketch \(y=\lvert ax+b\rvert\)}\par Sketch \(y=ax+b\). Keep the part on or above the \(x\)-axis and reflect the part below the axis upwards.\par Every output of a modulus function is non-negative.

transcription.tex: \textbf{1. Sketch \(y=\lvert2x-3\rvert\)}
The dotted line is \(y=2x-3\). Reflect its negative part upwards. The vertex is \((\tfrac32,0)\).
\textbf{2. Solve \(\lvert2x-3\rvert=5\)}
\[\begin{aligned}2x-3&=5\Rightarrow x=4,\\3-2x&=5\Rightarrow x=-1.\end{aligned}\]\par Both values are valid.
\textbf{3. Solve \(\lvert3x-5\rvert=2-\tfrac12x\)}
\[\begin{aligned}3x-5&=2-\tfrac12x\Rightarrow x=2,\\5-3x&=2-\tfrac12x\Rightarrow x=\tfrac65.\end{aligned}\]
\textbf{4. Solve \(\lvert3x-5\rvert>2-\tfrac12x\)}
The modulus graph lies above the line outside the intersections:\[x<\frac65\quad\text{or}\quad x>2.\]\par Strict inequality excludes both endpoints.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{1.} Solve \(\lvert x+1\rvert=2x+5\). There is only one solution.
For \(x\ge-1\), \(x+1=2x+5\) gives \(x=-4\), outside this branch, so reject it.\par For \(x<-1\):\[-x-1=2x+5\Rightarrow x=-2.\]\par Check: \(\lvert-2+1\rvert=1=2(-2)+5\).
\textbf{2.} Solve \(\lvert4x-1\rvert<2x\).

The boundary equations are\[\begin{aligned}4x-1&=2x\Rightarrow x=\tfrac12,\\1-4x&=2x\Rightarrow x=\tfrac16.\end{aligned}\]\par The blue graph is below the red line between the intersections:\[\frac16<x<\frac12.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{5.} \(g(x)=\lvert4-\tfrac32x\rvert\), \(h(x)=5\).\par (a) Sketch both graphs on the same axes.\par (b) Hence solve \(\lvert4-\tfrac32x\rvert=5\).
\[\begin{aligned}4-\tfrac32x&=5\Rightarrow x=-\tfrac23,\\\tfrac32x-4&=5\Rightarrow x=6.\end{aligned}\]\par The vertex is \((\tfrac83,0)\); the vertical intercept is 4.
\textbf{8.} Solve \(\lvert3x-5\rvert=11-x\).
\[\begin{aligned}5-3x&=11-x\Rightarrow x=-3,\\3x-5&=11-x\Rightarrow x=4.\end{aligned}\]\par Both values satisfy the original equation.
\textbf{9.} (a) On the same axes, sketch \(y=\lvert6-x\rvert\) and \(y=\tfrac12x-5\).\par (b) State, with a reason, whether \(\lvert6-x\rvert=\tfrac12x-5\) has any solutions.
There are no intersections, so no solutions.\par For \(x\le6\), the equation gives \(x=\tfrac{22}3>6\), outside that branch.\par For \(x\ge6\), it gives \(x=2<6\), again outside the branch.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{12.} Solve \(\lvert2x+9\rvert<14-x\).
\[\begin{aligned}-2x-9&=14-x\Rightarrow x=-23,\\2x+9&=14-x\Rightarrow x=\tfrac53.\end{aligned}\]\par The modulus graph lies below the line between the intersections:\[-23<x<\frac53.\]
\textbf{13.} The equation \(\lvert6-x\rvert=\tfrac12x+k\) has exactly one solution.\par (a) Find \(k\). (2 marks)\par (b) State the solution. (2 marks)
Exactly one intersection occurs at the vertex \((6,0)\):\[0=\tfrac12(6)+k\Rightarrow k=-3.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{What is a mapping?}\par A mapping relates a set of inputs to a set of outputs. It may follow a rule or be described by individual arrows.\par The \textbf{domain} is the set of possible inputs. The \textbf{range} is the set of outputs that are actually reached.

\textbf{An arbitrary mapping}\[0\mapsto4.4\text{ and }7.2,\qquad2\mapsto1,\qquad3.1\mapsto7.2.\]\par One input can relate to several outputs; different inputs can share an output. Some listed inputs may have no arrow.

\textbf{Example: \(x\mapsto2x\)}\[\begin{array}{c|rrrr}x&-1&0&1.7&2\\\hline2x&-2&0&3.4&4\end{array}\]\par A general relation may have more than one output for an input, or no output for some listed inputs. A function has a stricter rule, explored next.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{A function maps every element of its domain to exactly one output.}\par Notation: \(f(x)=2x+1\) or \(f:x\mapsto2x+1\). Here \(f(x)\) denotes the output for input \(x\).\par A graph represents the points \((x,f(x))\). The vertical line test checks whether an input has more than one output.
\textbf{A. This graph:}
Yes
No
Every vertical line meets the graph at most once.
\textbf{B. This graph:}
Yes
No
A positive input gives two outputs.
\textbf{C.} \(f(x)=2^x\)\par Domain: \(\mathbb R\).
Yes
No
Every real input has exactly one real output.
\textbf{D.} \(f(x)=\sqrt x\)\par Domain: \(\mathbb R\).
Yes
No
Negative inputs have no real output, so this domain is not valid.
\textbf{E.} \(f(x)=\pm\sqrt x\)\par Domain: \(x\ge0\).
Yes
No
For example, input 4 gives both 2 and \(-2\).

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: Each input of a function has one output. Different inputs may still share the same output. The horizontal line test distinguishes these two types.
\textbf{One-to-one}\par Every output in the range comes from exactly one input.\par Example: \(f(x)=2x+1\).
\(2\mapsto5,\quad3\mapsto7,\quad4\mapsto9\).\par No horizontal line intersects the graph more than once.
\textbf{Many-to-one}\par Two or more inputs can have the same output.\par Example: \(f(x)=x^2\), \(x\in\mathbb R\).
\(f(2)=4\) and \(f(-2)=4\).\par The horizontal line \(y=4\) intersects twice.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: Find each range and state whether the function is one-to-one or many-to-one. Use a sketch where helpful. Write ranges in terms of the output, not the input.
\[\begin{array}{c|rrrr}x&1&2&3&4\\\hline f(x)&1&4&7&10\end{array}\]\par Range: \(\{1,4,7,10\}\).\par One-to-one.
\textbf{(b)} \(g(x)=x^2\)\par Domain: \(-5\le x\le5\).
Range: \(0\le g(x)\le25\).\par Many-to-one.
\textbf{(c)} \(h(x)=1/x\)\par Domain: \(0<x\le3\).
Range: \(h(x)\ge\tfrac13\).\par One-to-one.

transcription.tex: A \textbf{piecewise function} uses different rules on different parts of its domain.\[f(x)=\begin{cases}5-2x,&x<1,\\x^2+3,&x\ge1.\end{cases}\]\par (a) Sketch \(y=f(x)\) and state the range.\par (b) Solve \(f(x)=19\).
The left branch approaches 3 but does not reach it. The right branch starts at 4. Together they give\[f(x)>3.\]\par An open circle excludes an endpoint; a filled circle includes it.

For \(x<1\): \(5-2x=19\Rightarrow x=-7\).\par For \(x\ge1\): \(x^2+3=19\Rightarrow x=\pm4\). Only \(x=4\) is in this branch.\par Therefore \(x=-7\) or \(x=4\).\par Reject \(x=-4\): it belongs to the unused part of the quadratic.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Edexcel C4 June 2012, Q6(a)}\par \(f(x)=e^x+2\), \(x\in\mathbb R\). State the range of \(f\).
Since \(e^x>0\), the range is \(f(x)>2\).\par The asymptote \(y=2\) is never reached.
\textbf{Edexcel C4 June 2010, Q4(d)}\par \(g(x)=x^2-4x+1\), \(0\le x\le5\). Find the range.
\(g(x)=(x-2)^2-3\), so the minimum is \(-3\) at \(x=2\).\par At the domain endpoints, \(g(0)=1\) and \(g(5)=6\).\par Hence \(-3\le g(x)\le6\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{7.} The function \(s\) is defined by\[s(x)=\begin{cases}x^2-6,&x<0,\\10-x,&x\ge0.\end{cases}\]\par (a) Sketch \(y=s(x)\).\par (b) Find all \(a\) such that \(s(a)=43\).\par (c) Solve \(s(x)=x\).
For \(a<0\): \(a^2-6=43\Rightarrow a=\pm7\); retain \(a=-7\).\par For \(a\ge0\): \(10-a=43\Rightarrow a=-33\), outside this branch.\par The only solution is \(a=-7\).
For \(x<0\):\[x^2-6=x\Rightarrow(x-3)(x+2)=0.\]Retain \(x=-2\).\par For \(x\ge0\): \(10-x=x\Rightarrow x=5\).\par Therefore \(x=-2\) or \(x=5\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{8.} The function \(p\) is defined by\[p(x)=\begin{cases}e^{-x},&-5\le x<0,\\x^3+4,&0\le x\le4.\end{cases}\]\par (a) Sketch \(y=p(x)\).\par (b) Find all \(a\), to 2 decimal places, such that \(p(a)=50\).
The left branch ends at the open point \((0,1)\); the right branch starts at the filled point \((0,4)\).

On the negative branch:\[e^{-a}=50\Rightarrow-a=\ln50\Rightarrow a=-3.91.\]\par On the non-negative branch:\[a^3+4=50\Rightarrow a=\sqrt[3]{46}=3.58.\]\par Both values lie within their branch domains.\par The solutions are \(a=-3.91\) and \(a=3.58\), to 2 decimal places.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{9.} The function \(h\) has domain \(-10\le x\le6\). It is linear from \((-10,14)\) to \((-4,2)\), and from \((-4,2)\) to \((6,27)\).\par (a) Sketch \(y=h(x)\).\par (b) State the range.\par (c) Find all \(a\) such that \(h(a)=12\).
The lowest output is 2 and the greatest is 27.\[2\le h(x)\le27.\]

The first segment has slope \(-2\), so \(h(x)=-2x-6\).\[-2a-6=12\Rightarrow a=-9.\]\par The second has slope \(\tfrac52\), so \(h(x)=\tfrac52x+12\).\[\tfrac52a+12=12\Rightarrow a=0.\]\par Both lie in the corresponding intervals.

transcription.tex: \textbf{11.} \(f(x)=ax^3+bx-5\), where \(a,b\) are constants. Given \(f(1)=-4\) and \(f(2)=9\), find \(a,b\).
\[\begin{aligned}a+b-5&=-4\Rightarrow a+b=1,\\8a+2b-5&=9\Rightarrow4a+b=7.\end{aligned}\]\par Subtracting gives \(3a=6\), so \(a=2\). Then \(2+b=1\), so \(b=-1\).
\textbf{12.} \(h(x)=x^2-6x+20\), with domain \(x\ge a\). Given that \(h\) is one-to-one, find the smallest possible \(a\). (6 marks)

\[h(x)=(x-3)^2+11.\]\par The vertex is \((3,11)\). The function is one-to-one on the increasing branch \(x\ge3\). Any smaller lower bound includes two inputs with the same output.\par Therefore the smallest possible value is \(a=3\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{Function or output?}\par Compare \(f:x\mapsto2x+1\) and \(f(x)=2x+1\).\par The first describes the mapping \(f\); the second gives its output for input \(x\). A variable can represent a function, just as it can represent a number, vector or set.
\textbf{Functional equations}\par Solving \(2x+1=5\) finds a number, \(x=2\). Solving\[f(x+y)=f(x)f(y)\]means finding functions that satisfy it.
One example is \(f(x)=2^x\), because\[2^{x+y}=2^x2^y.\]\par This verifies one solution; it does not find every possible function.

\textbf{Functions as inputs}\par A computer program can accept a function as an input. For example, applying \(x\mapsto x+1\) to every entry of \([1,2,3]\) gives \([2,3,4]\).\par A map operation builds a new list by applying \(f\) to each element of the original list.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Composite functions}\par Applying functions in succession creates a composite function.\[x\ \xrightarrow{\ f\ }\ f(x)\ \xrightarrow{\ g\ }\ g(f(x))\]\par \(gf(x)=g(f(x))\): apply \(f\) first, then \(g\).\par Read a composition from right to left. The order generally matters.
\textbf{Example}\par If \(f(x)=x+1\) and \(g(x)=2x\), compare \(gf(x)\) and \(fg(x)\).
\[gf(x)=2(x+1)=2x+2.\]\[fg(x)=2x+1.\]\par They are different functions.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: Let \(f(x)=x^2+1\) and \(g(x)=4x-2\). Replace each input of the outer function with the whole inner expression.
\textbf{(a)} Find \(fg(2)\).
\textbf{(b)} Find \(fg(x)\).
\textbf{(c)} Find \(gf(x)\).
\[\begin{aligned}gf(x)&=g(x^2+1)\\&=4(x^2+1)-2\\&=4x^2+2.\end{aligned}\]
\textbf{(d)} Find \(f^2(x)\).
\[f^2(x)=f(f(x))=(x^2+1)^2+1.\]\par Here \(f^2\) means apply \(f\) twice, not square its output.
\textbf{(e)} Solve \(gf(x)=38\).
\[\begin{aligned}4x^2+2&=38,\\x^2&=9,\\x&=\pm3.\end{aligned}\]

transcription.tex: \(f(x)=\lvert2x-8\rvert\), \(g(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{2}\).\par (a) Find \(fg(3)\).\par (b) Solve \(fg(x)=x\).

First form the composite:\[fg(x)=\left|2\left(\frac{x+1}{2}\right)-8\right|=\lvert x-7\rvert.\]\par For \(x<7\): \(7-x=x\Rightarrow x=\tfrac72\).\par For \(x\ge7\): \(x-7=x\) is impossible.\par The only solution is \(x=3.5\).

\[fg(x)=e^{\ln x}+2=x+2,\qquad x>0.\]\par Exponential and natural logarithm are inverse operations. The composite retains the restriction \(x>0\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{3.} \(f(x)=3x-2\), \(g(x)=x^2\), \(x\in\mathbb R\).\par (a) Find \(fg(x)\).\par (b) Solve \(fg(x)=gf(x)\).
\[\begin{aligned}3x^2-2&=(3x-2)^2,\\6x^2-12x+6&=0,\\(x-1)^2&=0.\end{aligned}\]\par Therefore \(x=1\).
\textbf{4.} \(p(x)=\dfrac1{x-2}\), \(x\ne2\), and \(q(x)=3x+4\), \(x\in\mathbb R\).\par (a) Express \(qp(x)\) as \(\dfrac{ax+b}{cx+d}\).\par (b) Solve \(qp(x)=16\).
\[qp(x)=\frac3{x-2}+4=\frac{4x-5}{x-2},\quad x\ne2.\]
\[\frac3{x-2}+4=16\Rightarrow x-2=\frac14.\]\par Hence \(x=\tfrac94\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{5.} \(f(x)=\lvert9-4x\rvert\), \(g(x)=\dfrac{3x-2}{2}\).\par (a) Find \(fg(6)\).\par (b) Solve \(fg(x)=x\).
\[g(6)=8,\qquad fg(6)=\lvert9-32\rvert=23.\]

\[fg(x)=\left|9-4\left(\frac{3x-2}{2}\right)\right|=\lvert13-6x\rvert.\]\par Solve each branch:\[13-6x=x\Rightarrow x=\frac{13}{7},\]\[6x-13=x\Rightarrow x=\frac{13}{5}.\]\par Both values satisfy \(fg(x)=x\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{MAT 2014, 1F}\par \(S(x)=x+1\), \(T(x)=-x\). Apply \(S\) a total of \(s\) times and \(T\) a total of \(t\) times, in some order, to obtain \(8-x\). What follows?\par (i) \(s=8,t=1\); (ii) \(s\) odd, \(t\) even; (iii) \(s\) even, \(t\) odd; (iv) both powers of 2; (v) none.

Each \(T\) reverses the coefficient of \(x\), so \(t\) is odd. Each \(S\) changes the constant’s parity; \(T\) preserves it. The final constant is even, so \(s\) is even.\par The counts are not unique. Therefore \textbf{(iii)}.

\textbf{MAT 2012, Q2}\par \(f(x)=x+1\), \(g(x)=2x\).\par (i) Show \(f^2g(x)=gf(x)\).\par (ii) Find all compositions giving \(4x+4\).\par (iii) Find \(f^igf^jgf^k(x)\), for integers \(i,j,k\ge0\).\par (iv) How many compositions give \(4x+4m\), where \(m\ge0\) is an integer?

(i) Both equal \(2x+2\).\par (ii) \(f^4g^2,\ f^2gfg,\ gf^2g,\ g^2f\).\par (iii) \(4x+4k+2j+i\).\par (iv) Require \(4k+2j+i=4m\). For each \(k=0,\ldots,m\), there are \(2(m-k)+1\) choices of \(j\), with \(i\) then fixed.\[1+3+\cdots+(2m+1)=(m+1)^2.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{Undoing a function}\par An inverse function reverses the original mapping. If \(f(4)=2\), then \(f^{-1}(2)=4\).\par For \(f(x)=2x+1\):\[x\xrightarrow{\times2}2x\xrightarrow{+1}2x+1.\]\par Undo the operations in reverse order: subtract 1, then divide by 2.\[f^{-1}(x)=\frac{x-1}{2}.\]
\textbf{Why must \(f\) be one-to-one?}
If two different inputs had the same output, reversing the arrows would give two outputs for one input. That would not be a function.

\textbf{Notation}\par \(f^{-1}\) means the inverse function; it does not mean \(1/f\).\par Similarly, \(\sin^{-1}\) denotes inverse sine.\par Applying \(f\), then \(f^{-1}\), returns the original input.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Method}\par Write \(y=f(x)\), make \(x\) the subject, then exchange the variable names.\par Example: \(y=2x+1\) gives \(x=\dfrac{y-1}{2}\), hence \(f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{2}\).
\textbf{1.} Find the inverse of \(f(x)=3-4x\).
\[\begin{aligned}y&=3-4x,\\4x&=3-y,\\x&=\frac{3-y}{4}.\end{aligned}\]\par Thus \(f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{3-x}{4}\).
\textbf{2.} Find the inverse of \(f(x)=\dfrac{x+2}{2x-1}\), \(x\ne\tfrac12\).
\[\begin{aligned}y(2x-1)&=x+2,\\x(2y-1)&=y+2,\\x&=\frac{y+2}{2y-1}.\end{aligned}\]\par Therefore \(f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{x+2}{2x-1}\), \(x\ne\tfrac12\). This function is its own inverse.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Reflect in \(y=x\)}\par Inverting swaps input and output: \((a,b)\) on \(y=f(x)\) becomes \((b,a)\) on \(y=f^{-1}(x)\).\par The graphs are reflections in \(y=x\). Vertical intercepts become horizontal intercepts; vertical asymptotes become horizontal ones.\par The domain of \(f\) is the range of \(f^{-1}\), and vice versa.
If the domain of \(f\) is \(x>1\), the range of \(f^{-1}\) is \(f^{-1}(x)>1\).
Illustration: blue \(f(x)=\ln(x-1)+2\); red \(f^{-1}(x)=e^{x-2}+1\). The dashed line is \(y=x\).

\[y=\sqrt{x-2}\Rightarrow x=y^2+2.\]\par Hence \(g^{-1}(x)=x^2+2\).
Domain: \(x\ge0\).\par Range: \(g^{-1}(x)\ge2\).

transcription.tex: \(f(x)=x^2-3\), with domain \(x\ge0\).\par (a) Find \(f^{-1}\).\par (b) Sketch both functions and state the domain of \(f^{-1}\).\par (c) Solve \(f(x)=f^{-1}(x)\).
\(y=x^2-3\Rightarrow x=\sqrt{y+3}\).\par Thus \(f^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{x+3}\), with domain \(x\ge-3\).
For this increasing function, intersections with its inverse lie on \(y=x\):\[x^2-3=x\Rightarrow x=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{13}}2.\]\par Since \(x\ge0\), retain \(x=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{13}}2\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{Edexcel C4 June 2012, Q6}\par \(f(x)=e^x+2\), \(x\in\mathbb R\).\par (d) Find \(f^{-1}\), stating its domain.\par (e) Sketch both curves on the same axes, giving all axis intercepts.
\[y=e^x+2\Rightarrow x=\ln(y-2).\]\par Thus \(f^{-1}(x)=\ln(x-2)\), with domain \(x>2\).

\(f\) crosses the vertical axis at \((0,3)\); it has no horizontal intercept.\par \(f^{-1}\) crosses the horizontal axis at \((3,0)\); it has no vertical intercept.\par The asymptotes are \(y=2\) and \(x=2\), respectively.
Blue: \(f\). Red: \(f^{-1}\). Dashed: \(y=x\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{3.} Explain why \(g:x\mapsto4-x\), with domain \(x>0\), is not identical to its inverse.
\[y=4-x\Rightarrow x=4-y.\]\par So the inverse has the same formula, \(g^{-1}(x)=4-x\). But a function includes its domain, not just its formula.

For \(g\): domain \(x>0\), range \(g(x)<4\).\par For \(g^{-1}\): domain \(x<4\), range \(g^{-1}(x)>0\).\par The domains differ, so the functions are not identical.\par For example, \(-1\) is a valid input for \(g^{-1}\), but not for \(g\).

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{5.} \(t(x)=x^2-6x+5\), with domain \(x\ge5\). Find \(t^{-1}(x)\).

Complete the square:\[y=(x-3)^2-4.\]\par As \(x\ge5\), take the positive square root:\[\sqrt{y+4}=x-3.\]\par Therefore\[t^{-1}(x)=3+\sqrt{x+4}.\]\par The range of \(t\) is \([0,\infty)\), so the inverse has domain \(x\ge0\).
Blue: \(t\). Red: \(t^{-1}\). The endpoints \((5,0)\) and \((0,5)\) are included.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{6.} \(m(x)=x^2+4x+9\), with domain \(x>a\), for a constant \(a\).\par (a) State the least value of \(a\) for which \(m^{-1}\) exists.\par (b) Find \(m^{-1}(x)\).\par (c) State its domain.
\[m(x)=(x+2)^2+5.\]\par The vertex is \((-2,5)\). Restricting to the right of the vertex makes the function one-to-one. The least value is \(a=-2\).
\[\begin{aligned}y&=(x+2)^2+5,\\\sqrt{y-5}&=x+2,\\x&=\sqrt{y-5}-2.\end{aligned}\]\par Thus \(m^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{x-5}-2\).
With \(a=-2\), the original domain is \(x>-2\), so the range is \(m(x)>5\).\par The inverse therefore has domain \(x>5\). The endpoint 5 is excluded.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{10.} \(f(x)=2x^2-3\), with domain \(x<0\).\par (a) Find \(f^{-1}(x)\), stating its domain.\par (b) Find the values of \(a\) for which \(f(a)=f^{-1}(a)\).
\[y=2x^2-3\Rightarrow x=-\sqrt{\frac{y+3}{2}}.\]\par Take the negative root because \(x<0\). Thus\[f^{-1}(x)=-\sqrt{\frac{x+3}{2}},\quad x>-3.\]

Solve the original equality:\[2a^2-3=-\sqrt{\frac{a+3}{2}}.\]\par It requires \(-3<a<0\) and \(2a^2-3<0\). Squaring gives\[8a^4-24a^2-a+15=0,\]\[ (a+1)(2a-3)(4a^2+2a-5)=0.\]\par Candidates: \(-1,\ \tfrac32,\ \tfrac{-1\pm\sqrt{21}}4\). Only \(a=-1\) satisfies the original equation: both sides equal \(-1\).
Always check roots after squaring. For a decreasing function, intersections with its inverse need not all lie on \(y=x\).

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{12.} \[f(x)=\frac{3(x+2)}{x^2+x-20}-\frac2{x-4},\quad x>4.\]\par (a) Show that \(f(x)=\dfrac1{x+5}\).\par (b) Find the range.\par (c) Find \(f^{-1}(x)\) and its domain.
\[\begin{aligned}f(x)&=\frac{3(x+2)-2(x+5)}{(x+5)(x-4)}\\&=\frac{x-4}{(x+5)(x-4)}\\&=\frac1{x+5},\quad x>4.\end{aligned}\]
For \(x>4\), the denominator satisfies \(x+5>9\), so\[0<f(x)<\frac19.\]\par Both endpoints are excluded.
\[y=\frac1{x+5}\Rightarrow x=\frac1y-5.\]\par Therefore\[f^{-1}(x)=\frac1x-5,\qquad0<x<\frac19.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{SMC 2008, Q25}\par Find the area of the region satisfying\[\bigl||x|-2\bigr|+\bigl||y|-2\bigr|\le4.\]\par A: 24 \quad B: 32 \quad C: 64\par D: 96 \quad E: 112

In the first quadrant, the inequality is\[|x-2|+|y-2|\le4.\]\par The full diamond has diagonals 8 and 8, so area 32. The two triangles outside the quadrant each have base 4 and height 2, so area 4.\par First-quadrant area: \(32-4-4=24\).\par By symmetry, the total area is\[4\times24=96.\]\par \textbf{Answer D.}
The boundary is included. The same area occurs in all four quadrants.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Two changes to one coordinate}\par For \(y=2f(x)+1\), vertical coordinates become \(2y+1\): multiply by 2, then add 1.\par For \(y=f(2x+1)\), solve \(2x_{\rm new}+1=x_{\rm old}\):\[x_{\rm new}=\frac{x_{\rm old}-1}{2}.\]\par Subtract 1, then halve. The order matters!
\textbf{Sketch \(y=\ln(1-2x)\)}

From \(y=\ln x\), horizontal coordinates map as\[x\mapsto\frac{1-x}{2}.\]\par Reflect and halve horizontally, then translate \(\tfrac12\) right.\par Domain: \(x<\tfrac12\). Vertical asymptote: \(x=\tfrac12\). Intercept: \((0,0)\). The graph is decreasing.

transcription.tex: \(f(x)=3|x-1|-2\), \(x\in\mathbb R\).\par \textbf{(b) State the range of \(f\).}
As \(|x-1|\ge0\),\[3|x-1|-2\ge-2.\]\par Equality holds at \(x=1\).\par Therefore the range is\[[-2,\infty),\quad\text{or }f(x)\ge-2.\]

transcription.tex: \(f(x)=3|x-1|-2\).\par \textbf{(c) Solve \(f(x)=\tfrac12x+3\).}
Blue: \(f(x)\). Red: \(\tfrac12x+3\). Split into branches at \(x=1\).
\textbf{For \(x\ge1\):}\[\begin{aligned}3(x-1)-2&=\tfrac12x+3,\\\tfrac52x&=8,\\x&=\frac{16}{5}.\end{aligned}\]\par This satisfies \(x\ge1\).
\textbf{For \(x<1\):}\[\begin{aligned}3(1-x)-2&=\tfrac12x+3,\\-\tfrac72x&=2,\\x&=-\frac47.\end{aligned}\]\par This satisfies \(x<1\). Both are valid.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Edexcel C4 June 2008, Q3}\par Given \(f(x)=2-|x+1|\):\par (c) Find \(P\), \(Q\) and \(R\). (3 marks)\par (d) Solve \(f(x)=\tfrac12x\). (5 marks)
At the maximum, \(|x+1|=0\), so \(P=(-1,2)\).\par At \(x=0\), \(f(0)=1\), so \(Q=(0,1)\).\par Solving \(|x+1|=2\) gives roots \(-3,1\). The right intercept is \(R=(1,0)\).
For \(x\ge-1\):\[2-(x+1)=\tfrac12x\Rightarrow x=\tfrac23.\]\par For \(x<-1\):\[2+(x+1)=\tfrac12x\Rightarrow x=-6.\]\par Both satisfy their branch conditions and the original equation.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 2G, Q8}\[h(x)=\tfrac23|x-1|-7,\quad x\in\mathbb R.\]\par (a) State the range. (1 mark)\par (b) Explain why \(h^{-1}\) does not exist. (1 mark)\par (c) Solve \(h(x)<-6\). (4 marks)\par (d) Find \(k\) for which \(h(x)=\tfrac23x+k\) has no solutions. (4 marks)
\(h(x)\ge-7\). The minimum is at \(x=1\).
\(h\) is many-to-one on \(\mathbb R\), so it has no inverse function on this domain.
\[\tfrac23|x-1|-7<-6\Rightarrow|x-1|<\tfrac32.\]\[-\tfrac12<x<\tfrac52.\]

The right branch is \(h(x)=\tfrac23x-\tfrac{23}3\), parallel to the given line. No intersection occurs when\[k<-\frac{23}3.\]\par At equality the entire right branch coincides; above it there is one intersection on the left.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 2G, Q9}\par \(h(x)=a-2|x+3|\), \(x\in\mathbb R\), crosses the vertical axis at \((0,4)\).\par (a) Find \(a\). (2 marks)\par (b) Find the maximum \(P\) and right-hand root \(Q\). (3 marks)\par (c) Solve \(h(x)=\tfrac13x+6\). (5 marks)

transcription.tex: \textbf{MAT 2006, Q1I}\par How many solutions does the equation\[|x|+|x-1|=0\]have?

Both terms are non-negative. Their sum could be zero only if both were zero.\par But \(|x|=0\) requires \(x=0\), whereas \(|x-1|=0\) requires \(x=1\). They cannot both hold.\par \textbf{There are no solutions.}
Alternatively, \(|x|+|x-1|\ge|x-(x-1)|=1\). The graph never reaches the horizontal axis.
